papers.title: Neural responses to food-related stimuli following experimental sleep manipulation: A systematic review of task-based neuroimaging studies.
papers.abstract: Adequate sleep is essential for physiological, cognitive, and mental functioning. While epidemiological and behavioral studies show that sleep restriction or sleep deprivation is associated with altered responses to food stimuli, the neural mechanisms underlying these effects remain unclear. The preregistered systematic review synthesized evidence from task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging studies examining neural responses to food-related stimuli following experimental sleep manipulations, including sleep deprivation or sleep restriction. Literature searches were conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and American Psychological Association PsycInfo, yielding 11 eligible studies, including nine with adult samples and two with adolescent samples. We extracted the data, assessed the risk of bias, and conducted a qualitative synthesis. Across studies with adult samples, six visual food-cue studies generally reported stronger brain activity following sleep deprivation or sleep restriction, particularly in the striatum, insula, anterior cingulate cortex, and inferior frontal gyrus. Two food valuation studies, including a willingness-to-pay and food-desire task, showed enhanced neural activity in the amygdala and hypothalamus during food valuation. Moreover, one study using a food odor perception paradigm showed that sleep deprivation altered chemosensory and interoceptive processing by enhancing food odor encoding in the piriform cortex. Two adolescent studies reported distinct neural findings. Together, these findings highlight that experimentally induced sleep deprivation or sleep restriction does not uniformly enhance reward-related brain activity; rather, it is associated with task-dependent changes in neural responses to food-related stimuli. However, the limited and heterogeneous evidence limits conclusions regarding common neural mechanisms. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

papers.title: Adaptive local temporal weighting for short-window EEG-based SSVEP recognition using FB-eTRCA.
papers.abstract: To improve short-window SSVEP recognition, we integrated adaptive temporal local weighting (ATLW) with filter-bank ensemble task-related component analysis (FB-eTRCA). ATLW estimates local discriminability from training trials, converts window scores into sample weights, and applies the training-derived weights to training and test trials within each cross-validation fold. Experiments were conducted on two public 40-target SSVEP datasets: the Benchmark dataset containing 35 subjects and six blocks, and the BETA database containing 70 subjects and four blocks. Seven observation windows ranging from 0.2 to 1.4 s were evaluated using subject-specific leave-one-block-out validation, with six folds for the Benchmark dataset and four folds for the BETA database. On the Benchmark dataset, only the 0.2-s accuracy gain remained significant after Holm correction (44.79% vs 44.07%; adjusted p = 0.0300); other windows were nonsignificant. On the Benchmark dataset, ablation analysis showed that adaptive weighting was more stable than fixed temporal weighting. After Holm correction, eTRCA+ATLW significantly outperformed eTRCA at 0.4 s (gain: 0.86 percentage points; adjusted p = 0.0023), but not at 0.2 s, supporting transferability to another TRCA-based decoder. EEGNet and BiLSTM were included as representative CNN and RNN baselines; both performed below the TRCA-family methods under the present subject-specific limited-calibration protocol. On the BETA database, FB-eTRCA+ATLW remained close to FB-eTRCA across all seven observation windows without BETA-specific parameter retuning, but no paired difference was statistically significant. These findings indicate that ATLW is a lightweight temporal refinement that can be applied to more than one TRCA-based decoder. Its measurable benefit may depend on SSVEP signal quality and the amount of available subject-specific calibration data. Accuracy increased with longer windows, whereas the information transfer rate peaked at 0.6 s on the Benchmark dataset. Therefore, no observation window was optimal for both accuracy and communication speed.

papers.title: NaV1.8 Inhibition and the Future of Nonopioid Analgesia in Otolaryngology: A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Postoperative pain management in otolaryngology requires balancing effective analgesia while minimizing adverse effects, such as opioid-related complications. Suzetrigine is a first-in-class selective voltage-gated sodium channel (NaV1.8) inhibitor that has been recently approved by the US Food and Drug Administration. Suzetrigine selectively inhibits NaV1.8 channels expressed in peripheral nociceptive neurons, thereby reducing pain signaling without the respiratory depression, sedation, or misuse potential associated with opioids. This review summarizes the pharmacology, efficacy, safety profile, limitations, and potential applications of suzetrigine in otolaryngology. Prospective clinical trials consist of 2 phase 2 randomized clinical trials, 2 phase 3 randomized placebo-controlled trials, and 1 phase 3 open-label study involving more than 3000 patients. Across abdominoplasty and bunionectomy pain models, suzetrigine demonstrated superior analgesia compared with placebo and mixed efficacy comparable to hydrocodone/acetaminophen. The drug was generally well tolerated, with adverse event rates similar to placebo and no significant respiratory, cardiac, or sedating adverse effects reported. Additionally, 1 retrospective cohort study has reported results in patients undergoing free flap reconstruction and transoral robotic surgery. Suzetrigine is a promising nonopioid analgesic with demonstrated efficacy compared to placebo in acute postoperative pain and a favorable safety profile. In otolaryngology, suzetrigine may serve as an adjunct to multimodal analgesia and an opioid-sparing option for patients with contraindications to traditional analgesics, opioid use disorder, or procedures that are expected to have high opioid utilization such as tonsillectomy, sleep surgery, and major head and neck surgery. Future studies in otolaryngology are warranted to evaluate whether suzetrigine can meaningfully reduce postoperative opioid exposure without compromising analgesic effectiveness.

papers.title: Intracranial EEG for Detecting Epileptic Activity in Acute Brain Injury: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) has been increasingly explored as part of multimodal neuromonitoring in acute brain injury, yet its diagnostic benefit compared with continuous surface EEG (suEEG) remains uncertain. We have performed a meta-analysis to quantify seizure and rhythmic and periodic pattern detection rates and concordance with suEEG. Secondary objectives were the assessment of correlations with brain injury, safety, and techniques. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, and Embase were searched for studies reporting iEEG monitoring in adults with acute brain injury. Epileptic patterns were harmonized to the American Clinical Neurophysiology Society Standardized EEG Nomenclature for Critically Ill Patients (ACNS) 2021 terminology, classifying events as seizures/status epilepticus (SZ/SE) or rhythmic and periodic/ictal-interictal continuum patterns (RPP/IIC). Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa scale and custom bias domains. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted for (i) pooled proportions and (ii) pooled paired within-patient comparisons. Twelve cohorts (n = 864 participants) with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (n = 343), traumatic brain injury (n = 351), and mixed etiologies (n = 170) were included. Six studies provided paired iEEG-suEEG data (n = 273). Techniques were based on a strip or depth electrode. No severe adverse events were reported. Pooled iEEG versus suEEG incidence rates were respectively: 26% vs. 15% for SZ/SE, 47% vs. 34% for RPP/IIC, and 57% vs. 37% for clinically relevant epileptic activity. Pooled paired analysis demonstrated that iEEG additionally detected SZ/SE in 16.5% of patients [pooled McNemar odds ratio (OR) 3.46 (0.51-23.6); I2 = 63%; p = 0.158] and RPP/IIC in 26% [pooled OR 4.25 (0.19-96.1); I2 = 73%; p = 0.236], while suEEG was negative. Sensitivity analyses for high-risk studies or cohort overlap did not alter the results. Invasive EEG monitoring substantially increased the detection of seizures and RPP/IIC patterns compared with suEEG alone in patients with acute brain injury, serving as a promising monitoring adjunct.

papers.title: Postoperative hemorrhage and perioperative outcomes in single-port versus multi-port transoral robotic surgery for upper airway disease.
papers.abstract: The integration of transoral robotic surgery (TORS) has catalyzed a paradigm shift in the management of upper airway pathologies; however, the multifaceted operational distinctions between next-generation single-port (SP) platforms and conventional multi-port systems warrant comprehensive investigation. This retrospective analysis delves into the perioperative metrics and postoperative hemorrhage profiles of 126 patients undergoing TORS via the Si, Xi, and SP platforms. Procedures were categorized by complexity as single- or multilevel. To mitigate baseline confounders, we engineered a propensity-matched cohort of multilevel cases (n = 21 per platform). Overall, major postoperative hemorrhage manifested in 9.5% of the cohort. As anticipated, multilevel interventions underscored significant increases in operative duration, postoperative pain, and hospitalization length. In our unmatched analysis, the SP platform demonstrated a robust safety profile, yielding an overall hemorrhage rate of merely 3.1% (0% in single-level; 4.8% in multilevel), contrasting with higher incidences in the Si and Xi cohorts. Within the intricately matched multilevel subset, the SP system showcased significantly fewer major hemorrhage events compared to the Xi platform (4.8% vs. 28.6%). Crucially, this synergy cannot be solely attributed to robotic mechanics, as topical hemostatic agents were universally leveraged in matched SP cases. Exploratory hierarchical Firth penalized logistic regression illuminated that incorporating the robotic platform significantly augmented the predictive model (Firth p = 0.048), indicating the SP platform is associated with reduced hemorrhage odds (adjusted odds ratio = 0.22). Ultimately, this compelling evidence sheds light on the SP system's potential to optimize safety in complex airway reconstruction, necessitating future standardized prospective trials.

papers.title: It's about time: modeling circadian regulation of cardiac electrophysiology and arrhythmogenesis.
papers.abstract: Cardiac electrophysiology models resolve processes ranging from millisecond-scale ion-channel gating to hour-scale protein trafficking; yet, most do not explicitly represent circadian time. Consequently, ion-channel conductance, autonomic input, body temperature, and clock-regulated gene expression are often treated as fixed parameters or time-invariant inputs, causing simulated cardiac cells to correspond to an implicit and potentially arbitrary biological phase. In vivo, however, these factors vary across the ∼24-h cycle and jointly shape sinoatrial nodal pacemaking, ventricular repolarization, arrhythmia susceptibility, and drug response. In this mini-review, we examine recent efforts to incorporate circadian regulation into computational models of cardiac electrophysiology, including sinoatrial nodal and ventricular myocyte models of pacemaking, arrhythmogenesis, seizure-induced sinus arrhythmias, and drug-induced proarrhythmic risk. We synthesize these studies using a layered "source-transfer-target" organization in which intrinsic and systemic circadian sources act through source-specific transfer processes-including transcription, translation, channel trafficking, receptor-mediated signaling, and direct thermal modulation-to regulate shared electrophysiological targets. Building on this synthesis, we propose a general current-level formulation for incorporating circadian regulation of maximal conductance, channel gating, and ionic driving force into Hodgkin-Huxley-type models. Finally, we identify the experimental, computational, and clinical advances needed to translate these formulations into human-specific, personalized models of cardiac rhythm and arrhythmogenesis, with the long-term goal of enabling circadian-aware cardiac digital twins for time-resolved risk prediction and chronotherapeutic optimization.
papers.journal: American journal of physiology. Cell physiology

papers.title: "Frontal Slow-Wave Asymmetry in Obstructive Sleep Apnea and Its Modulation During CPAP Titration".
papers.abstract: Sleep slow-wave activity (SWA) shows regional and hemispheric variation reflecting local cortical regulation. Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) introduces recurrent respiratory instability and arousals that may alter cortical dynamics during sleep. It remains unclear whether continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) affects hemispheric SWA balance. In this retrospective observational study, we included adult patients who underwent diagnostic polysomnography followed by a CPAP titration study on a separate night. Frontal delta power during N3 sleep was calculated from F3-A2 and F4-A1 using spectral analysis. Hemispheric asymmetry was quantified using a normalized asymmetry index (F4 - F3) / (F4 + F3). Sleep, respiratory, and EEG parameters were compared using paired nonparametric tests. A total of 143 patients were included (median age 47 years, 76% male). CPAP improved respiratory parameters, with median apnea-hypopnea index decreasing from 27.4 to 3.2 events/h (P < .001). Frontal delta power decreased at both F3 and F4 during CPAP (P < .001). Absolute asymmetry index decreased from 9.35% to 7.55% (P = .008). Signed asymmetry shifted toward left hemispheric dominance (P < .001). Right-dominant patterns were more frequent during the diagnostic night, whereas left-dominant patterns predominated during CPAP. Among patients with non-neutral asymmetry on both nights, dominance direction changed significantly (McNemar P = .008), mainly from right to left. CPAP is associated with reduced frontal delta power and attenuation of hemispheric SWA asymmetry during deep sleep, suggesting that respiratory stabilization may influence cortical organization. These findings should be interpreted considering potential night-to-night effects.

papers.title: Bounded Autonomy or Unbounded Work? Work-Time Control, Boundary Intrusion, and Exhaustion in the Korean Working Conditions Survey.
papers.abstract: We examined whether work during free time was associated with greater exhaustion among workers with high work-time control. Wage employees aged 18-64 years in the 2023 (n=22,036) and 2020 (n=23,971) Korean Working Conditions Surveys were analyzed. Four profiles combined work-time control and work during free time. Survey-weighted models estimated differences in a two-item exhaustion score, adjusting for demographic and work factors. The 2023 comparison was primary; the 2020 comparison assessed reproducibility. Among workers with high control, repeated work during free time (unbounded autonomy) was associated with greater exhaustion than rare or no such work (bounded autonomy) in 2023 (β=0.36, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.61) and 2020 (β=0.31, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.59). The interaction with control was not significant in 2023 (P = .600) but was negative in 2020 (P = .008). Sensitivity analyses supported the 2023 association; in 2020, confidence intervals under both weekly-or-more definitions included zero. Unbounded autonomy was also associated with sleep disturbance and work-to-family conflict. Repeated work during free time was associated with greater exhaustion even among workers with high work-time control. Control did not consistently modify this association across waves. These cross-sectional findings support considering work during free time alongside scheduling flexibility.

papers.title: Rhythmic Timekeeping in Rice: Emerging Mechanisms and Regulatory Networks.
papers.abstract: The circadian clock is an endogenous time-keeping mechanism found in most eukaryotes that integrates external signals to synchronize biological processes with the environment. Circadian and diel rhythms across multiple regulatory layers help coordinate gene expression underlying plant processes such as metabolism, stress responses, and agronomic traits. In the context of a changing environment, a comprehensive understanding of how circadian-mediated regulatory mechanisms can contribute to plant resilient strategies continues to be a priority. In this mini review, we highlight the pleiotropic functions of the rice circadian clock in coordinating diverse processes.

papers.title: Photography training and inhibitory control: ERP correlates and dissociable patterns from athletic training.
papers.abstract: Long‑term engagement in professional behavioral training and the resulting behavioral changes are known to influence human cognition. The present study investigates whether and how photography training is associated with individuals' inhibitory control. Fifteen photographers, 15 athletes, and 15 controls were recruited to complete a Go/Nogo task with concurrent electroencephalogram recording. Behavioral results showed slower response times and fewer commission errors for both photographers and athletes compared with controls, with no significant difference between the two training groups. Event‑related potential analyses revealed more negative Bereitschaftspotential amplitudes and more positive N2 amplitudes for photographers and athletes than for controls, again with no significant difference between photographers and athletes. Furthermore, a more negative prefrontal negativity amplitude was observed for athletes than for both photographers and controls, whereas no significant difference was found between photographers and controls. Photography training was associated with a shift in the speed-accuracy trade‑off toward a greater emphasis on accuracy, as well as motor preparation and conflict monitoring-two core subprocesses of inhibitory control. Moreover, photographers and athletes showed improvements in inhibitory control through different neurocognitive pathways: while both groups showed enhanced motor preparation and conflict monitoring, athletes additionally exhibited enhanced cognitive preparation compared with photographers. This differential pattern may reflect athletes' need to respond to unpredictable, real‑time emergencies during competition.

papers.title: Longitudinal Sleep Spindle Maturation Trajectories and Their Association With Internalizing Problems in Adulthood.
papers.abstract: Extensive cortical refinement from childhood to adulthood coincides with heightened vulnerability to internalizing problems, such as anxiety and depression. Thalamocortical sleep spindles may provide neurophysiological indices of such vulnerability. In this longitudinal study (2009-2023), we examined developmental trajectories of slow (11-13 Hz) and fast (13-15 Hz) spindle density across childhood (≈9.5 years), adolescence (≈16 years) and young adulthood (≈22.5 years), and tested whether individual differences in these trajectories were associated with internalizing problems during adulthood. At each wave, participants completed two nights of ambulatory polysomnography (N = 28; 19 female). Internalizing problems were assessed using five standardized self-report and external-report questionnaires. Slow spindle density declined between childhood and adulthood, with a posterior-to-anterior pattern characterized by earlier centroparietal and later frontal reductions. Fast spindle density globally increased from childhood to adolescence and then stabilized. Associations with internalizing problems were specific to slow spindle development: more internalizing problems were linked to a steeper decline in widespread slow spindle density from childhood to adolescence. Because questionnaire measures showed no evidence of developmental change in our sample, this association reflects interindividual differences rather than symptom emergence. These findings indicate that a steeper decline in slow spindle density from childhood to adolescence is associated with more internalizing problems, underscoring the importance of a developmental perspective when linking sleep spindles to emotional functioning.

papers.title: GABAergic subiculum-medial entorhinal projection in mice and rats.
papers.abstract: The subiculum (SUB) is a major hippocampal output hub that routes information to cortical and subcortical targets, and its long-range projections are considered excitatory. Using enhancer-driven adeno-associated viral vectors to selectively label γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-releasing neurons across species, here we show that the dorsal SUB also sends an inhibitory projection to the dorsal part of the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) in mice and rats. Anterograde tracing in mice revealed that the dorsal SUB contains GABAergic neurons that project sparsely to all layers of the dorsal MEC with enrichment in superficial layers, in contrast to the glutamatergic SUB axons targeting MEC layer V. Slice electrophysiology demonstrated that these GABAergic axons form inhibitory synapses in the MEC. A subset of projecting neurons expressed parvalbumin (PV), whereas somatostatin-positive neurons were infrequent. Consistently, PV neuron-specific anterograde tracing recapitulated the SUB-to-MEC projection. In rats, subicular GABAergic axons were enriched in MEC layer II, and SynaptoTAG2-labeled presynaptic boutons were positive for the vesicular GABA transporter, supporting inhibitory synapse formation. Anterograde tracing of PV neurons similarly recapitulated the laminar axonal distribution in the MEC. These results identify a conserved PV-associated inhibitory SUB-to-MEC projection with specific laminar organization, extending the canonical excitatory view of subicular output.

papers.title: Teamwork in Parkinson's care: Building multidisciplinary models worldwide.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a complex, progressive neurodegenerative disorder requiring comprehensive, long-term management. PD affects millions of people globally and presents with motor and non-motor symptoms that progressively impair function and quality of life. While pharmacological therapy remains effective, optimal care extends beyond medication management. Traditional care models for PD often rely heavily on doctors and primarily target motor symptoms and motor complications, with less attention to non-motor symptoms, many of which remain under-recognized. This imbalance contributes to fragmented care and unmet patient needs. These challenges highlight the need for a multidisciplinary care team to address the full spectrum of patient needs. Therefore, integrating a multidisciplinary approach is essential for comprehensive PD management. This manuscript proposes a scalable, multidisciplinary care team model designed to optimise clinical outcomes, enhance quality of life, and remain adaptable across diverse healthcare systems worldwide. It addresses global challenges associated with MDT implementation and outlines potential future solutions. The manuscript also highlights stakeholder engagement in Community Engagement and Involvement (CEI), including initiatives in Tanzania and Thailand to raise community awareness. In particular, the "CheckPD" project and integrated "eat, move, sleep" lifestyle interventions promote lifestyle-based strategies for PD prevention and improved long-term management of PD. Overall, the model emphasises coordinated, patient-centred care that integrates medical, rehabilitative, psychological, and social support services.

papers.title: Near Real-Time Quantitative Ultrasound Imaging Using an Ultra-Portable Handheld Ultrasound System.
papers.abstract: Clinical ultrasound is widely used because of its low cost, portability, safety, and real-time imaging capability, making it well suited for point-of-care applications. However, conventional B-mode imaging is inherently qualitative and primarily sensitive to tissue morphology. Quantitative ultrasound (QUS) methods exploit information contained in backscattered radiofrequency (RF) signals to extract fundamental acoustic tissue properties, such as the backscatter coefficient (BSC) and attenuation, which more directly quantify tissue microstructure and provide complementary information to B-mode imaging. Although QUS methods have been implemented on conventional cart-based ultrasound scanners, their integration into portable handheld systems remains limited. Motivated by the growing availability and clinical potential of ultra-portable ultrasound devices, this protocol presents a QUS imaging pipeline implemented on the DKPOC probe (portable linear ultrasound probe; Vermon SA, Tours, France), which interfaces directly with a laptop through a USB-C connection. The protocol integrates multiple QUS processing methods based on spectral analysis and envelope statistics of RF data acquired using focused-wave or plane-wave transmit modes. QUS processing begins with a user-defined region of interest (ROI). The reference phantom method is used to estimate the BSC and attenuation within sliding sub-ROIs. Model-based fitting of the estimated BSC is then performed to extract tissue microstructure-related parameters, including effective scatterer diameter and effective acoustic concentration. In addition, envelope statistics parameters are estimated using three probability density functions. Computed QUS parameter maps are displayed as translucent color overlays on corresponding B-mode images. The workflow is implemented in a numerical computing software-based graphical user interface, enabling near real-time QUS processing, parameter map visualization, interactive parameter adjustment, and rapid evaluation of different processing configurations. The pipeline is adaptable to different imaging sequences and ultrasound probes, providing a practical framework for quantitative point-of-care ultrasound imaging and clinician-led QUS studies in human subjects.

papers.title: Sex-Specific Differences in Symptomatology and Quality of Life Impact of Allergic Rhinitis: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Allergic Rhinitis (AR) is a widespread condition that significantly affects the quality of life (QOL) of those affected globally. It contributes to sleep disturbances, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, and can worsen symptoms in individuals with coexisting asthma. This study examines the impact of AR on QOL in adults, with specific attention to sex differences. A cross-sectional online survey using a purpose-designed, non-validated questionnaire was distributed via social media using convenience sampling to 1572 Jordanian adults. The questionnaire collected data on demographics, AR symptoms, triggers, and the impact of AR on mental health, social functioning, and daily life. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Chi-square tests. Multivariable logistic regression was used to adjust for potential confounders, and Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied to account for multiplicity. A total of 1572 respondents participated; 683 (43.4%) had physician-diagnosed AR. AR was reported by 157/419 males (37.5%) and 526/1153 females (45.6%); this sex difference was statistically significant (χ2 = 8.31, p = 0.004; OR = 1.40, 95% CI 1.11-1.76). Most patients lived in urban areas (69.4%). While sneezing and rhinorrhoea were common across sexes, females reported significantly higher rates of nasal itching/congestion (55.5% vs. 43.9%, p = 0.011), headaches (61.0% vs. 43.9%, p < 0.001), and increased stress/anxiety (53.4% vs. 42.7%, p = 0.018, not surviving false discovery rate (FDR) correction). In contrast, snoring was more prevalent in males (40.1% vs. 24.1%, p < 0.001). Regarding QOL, AR severely disrupted sleep (80.7%) and concentration (66.2%) for both sexes. However, females were significantly more likely to report irritability/emotional distress (65.4% vs. 55.4%, p = 0.023), prefer social isolation during symptoms (59.3% vs. 47.8%, p = 0.010), and experience limitations in activities outside the home (55.1% vs. 45.9%, p = 0.041). After adjustment, female sex remained significantly associated with irritability/emotional distress (aOR = 1.50, 95% CI 1.02-2.22, p = 0.039) and preference for social isolation (aOR = 1.53, 95% CI 1.05-2.23, p = 0.028). After Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction, nasal itching/congestion, snoring, and headache remained statistically significant in symptom analyses; no QOL items survived FDR correction, and these findings should be considered exploratory. Asthma was reported by 80/683 (11.7%) of AR patients, more frequently among males than females (19.7% vs. 9.3%, p < 0.001). Sensitivity analyses showed that the association between female sex and social isolation was robust to adjustment for or exclusion of asthma, whereas the association with irritability was attenuated after excluding participants with asthma. These findings suggest AR's substantial impact on daily functioning and mental well-being, with signals of greater psychosocial burden among women. Improved understanding of sex-specific challenges can support more effective prevention, diagnosis, and management strategies, with tailored strategies to address the distinct symptom burden and QOL impairments experienced by female patients. These findings may provide preliminary insights into the burden of AR in Jordan and should be confirmed in representative, validated surveys.

papers.title: Associations of meal timing and dietary macronutrient timing with sleep quality in a diet and physical activity intervention: The Sistas Inspiring Sistas through Activity and Support (SISTAS) study.
papers.abstract: BackgroundChrononutrition emphasizes alignment of meal timing with circadian rhythms, as misalignment of eating and sleep behaviors may adversely affect health.AimWe examined the relationship between timing of dietary macronutrients and sleep quality.MethodsThis post hoc analysis used data from the Sistas Inspiring Sistas through Activity and Support randomized trial. Participants completed the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and a 24-h dietary recall at baseline (n = 251), 3 months (n = 159), and 12 months (n = 127). Meal-timing metrics included clock times for meals and the percentage of daily macronutrient intake consumed after 5 p.m. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for relevant covariates.SummaryLater breakfast timing was associated with poorer sleep quality at 12 months (β = 0.64, p = 0.02). No significant associations were observed for lunch or dinner timing, or macronutrient intake after 5 p.m. Later breakfast timing may be associated with lower sleep quality. Further studies should explore meal timing and composition in diverse populations.

papers.title: Perioperative Neurocognitive Disorders in Older Adults: Mechanisms, Biomarkers, and Evidence-Informed Management.
papers.abstract: Perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PNDs) encompass cognitive change identified before or after surgery. Postoperative delirium (POD) is an acute, fluctuating disorder of attention and awareness, whereas delayed neurocognitive recovery and postoperative mild or major neurocognitive disorder describe objectively assessed decline over longer intervals. This narrative review focuses on older adults undergoing noncardiac and cardiac surgery and examines neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, neurotransmitter imbalance, oxidative stress, synaptic dysfunction, candidate fluid biomarkers, and electroencephalography (EEG) features, and evidence-informed management. Multicomponent prevention, medication review, mobilization, sleep support, and individualized anesthetic care remain the most defensible clinical strategies. EEG-guided anesthetic titration can reduce anesthetic exposure but has not consistently reduced POD. Blood biomarkers, machine-learning models, trial-by-trial neural variability, and noninvasive brain stimulation are promising research tools, but none currently replaces standardized clinical assessment or justifies routine mechanism-specific treatment.

papers.title: Reduced Brain Complexity During the Execution of a Sequential Arm Movement Following an Augmented-Feedback-Based Practice: A Multiscale Entropy Analysis.
papers.abstract: Motor learning is accompanied by adaptive changes in neural processing, yet the extent to which feedback-based practice alters the complexity of cortical activity during movement execution remains unclear. The present study examined learning-associated changes in brain complexity during the execution of a sequential arm movement following augmented-feedback-based practice. Thirty-eight healthy young adults practiced a sequential arm movement with augmented feedback across five sessions. Cortical activity was recorded with electroencephalography during the first and last practice sessions. Multiscale entropy was used to quantify brain complexity across 50 time scales. Behavioral measures indicated improved movement accuracy and reduced dual-task costs across practice. At the cortical level, a significant global decrease in entropy was observed from the first to the last practice session. Further analyses revealed that the differences were confined to coarse temporal window and midline frontal electrodes Fz and FCz. In addition, changes in coarse-scale entropy at FCz were negatively correlated with reductions in absolute error. Together, the present findings suggest that augmented-feedback-based practice is accompanied by a refinement of cortical complexity during movement execution, particularly in large-scale frontal dynamics. Multiscale entropy may therefore provide a sensitive framework for capturing learning-related neural adaptations that complement conventional electroencephalographic measures and advance the understanding of motor learning at the systems level.

papers.title: A cross-species comparison of excitation energy transfer in red-lineage photosystem I.
papers.abstract: The photosystem I supercomplex (PSI) is a central component of photosynthesis in plants and algae. Its antenna subunits absorb light and transfer the excitation energy through an interconnected pigment network to the reaction center (RC), where it is converted to chemical energy. Although the excitation energy transfer (EET) in photosystems has been well characterized for individual organisms, evolutionary variation and inconsistent modeling settings have obscured cross-species comparisons, and it remains unclear which common structural features sustain EET efficiency. To address this, we combined kinetic modeling and rate theories to simulate EET processes in multiple red-lineage PSI complexes, each consisting of hundreds of chlorophylls, using the same set of experiment-derived parameters. We performed network analysis to probe how their EET processes respond to structural variation across distinct species. The exciton becomes increasingly delocalized as it approaches the core region of the PSI complexes. This, together with a radial site-energy bias, creates a strong exciton energy gradient (EEG) that funnels the exciton to the RC. However, the EEG is effective only over a limited distance range from the core region. In large PSI complexes, the pigments farther from the RC are weakly coupled, and the efficiency of long-range EET is maintained by additional features that complement the EEG, such as the pigment composition in the peripheral regions of the antenna, which also broadens the energy range of light absorption. By comparing red-lineage PSI complexes with a common parameter set, we provide a framework for relating EET to structural rearrangements in the pigment network.

papers.title: Non-invasive neuromodulation after repetitive head impacts: current evidence and a precision framework for circuit-based rehabilitation.
papers.abstract: Repetitive head impacts (RHIs) are associated with heterogeneous cognitive, behavioral, psychiatric, sleep-related, pain, and neurological symptoms. Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) remains a postmortem neuropathological diagnosis, whereas traumatic encephalopathy syndrome (TES) is a clinical research syndrome assessed during life. No intervention has been shown to modify CTE pathology, but neuromodulation may support the surviving neural circuits. PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus and Google Scholar were searched from database inception to August 2026 for this narrative review. The author evaluates magnetic and electrical stimulation, low-intensity ultrasound, photobiomodulation and cranial nerve stimulation as adjuncts to rehabilitation after repetitive head impacts. Direct RHI/TES evidence is distinguished from findings in other traumatic brain injury and concussion populations, other clinical populations and experimental models. The author then proposes a phenotype- and circuit-guided framework for treatment development. Neuromodulation should not be considered a disease-modifying treatment for CTE. Its most credible role is as a phenotype-led adjunct to rehabilitation. This approach requires identification of a viable circuit relevant to the dominant impairment, selection of an individualized stimulation dose, measurement of target engagement and pairing with symptom-relevant rehabilitation. Progress requires credible sham-controlled and factorial trials, multimodal biomarkers, clinically meaningful functional outcomes, and long-term follow-up.

papers.title: [Association of the rs1801260 T>C polymorphism of the CLOCK gene with sleep quality and buccal epithelial DNA damage in schoolchildren in the Arctic: A pilot study].
papers.abstract: To assess the impact of the rs1801260 T>C polymorphism in the CLOCK gene and environmental light conditions on sleep quality and cytogenetic instability among children living at high latitudes. The study included 77 schoolchildren aged 15 to 17 years (mean age 15.4 years; 58.4% female). The rs1801260 polymorphism in the CLOCK gene was analyzed using buccal epithelial samples collected from healthy participants. Individuals with the CC genotype at the rs1801260 polymorphism of the CLOCK gene exhibited a higher frequency of nuclear protrusions and reduced sleep quality compared to carriers of the T allele. The rs1801260 polymorphism in the CLOCK gene may be associated with increased sensitivity to genotoxic environmental factors.
papers.journal: Zhurnal nevrologii i psikhiatrii imeni S.S. Korsakova

papers.title: [Pseudo-remission in childhood absence epilepsy. Objective assessment of seizure control and the role of ethosuximide].
papers.abstract: Absence epilepsy is a common form of pseudo-remission, in which patients and observers may incorrectly believe seizures have ceased while paroxysms persist in subtle form. Three primary factors contribute to this phenomenon: the brief duration (typically less than 10 seconds) and indistinct semiology of typical absences; the limited reliability of parental observation (sensitivity up to 43%); and the occurrence of generalized spike-wave discharges without significant clinical manifestations, which are nonetheless associated with fluctuations in wakefulness. Verification of remission requires at least a properly conducted three-minute hyperventilation test with attentional load. Preferred methods for objective assessment include prolonged video-EEG monitoring that registers wakefulness, sleep, and arousal, and, when indicated, intermittent photic stimulation. However, no direct comparative studies have demonstrated superiority of these methods over short-term EEG with adequately performed hyperventilation. Extended EEG monitoring does not substitute for the induction of provoking factors, and functional testing does not obviate the need for sufficient recording duration. The absence of "peak-slow wave" discharges lasting three seconds or longer may serve as a practical operational criterion, as adopted from the CAE study protocol. Data are presented on the proportion of patients free from treatment failure with ethosuximide, valproic acid, and lamotrigine in patients with newly diagnosed childhood absence epilepsy at Week 16 (53%, 58%, and 29%, respectively) and at Month 12 (45%, 44%, and 21%, respectively). The review also describes the mechanism of action of ethosuximide, discrepancies between NICE recommendations and Russian clinical guidelines, dosing considerations, and the need for laboratory monitoring. The clinical benefit of adjusting therapy based on EEG findings in patients with apparent clinical well-being remains unproven.

papers.title: [Increased nervous excitability, anxiety, and sleep disorders in childhood - the role of multicomponent low-dose medications].
papers.abstract: Anxiety, emotional excitability, and sleep disturbances are common in pediatric populations, often emerging during stressful periods such as chronic family conflict, parental divorce, initial socialization in kindergarten, and the beginning of formal schooling. These conditions are frequently linked to autonomic nervous system (ANS) dysfunction. During such periods, nervous system instability impairs stress adaptation and may lead to neurotic reactions. Chronic stress and anxiety can trigger neuroinflammatory processes, which further intensify anxiety and ANS dysfunction. Clinically, these mechanisms present as autonomic disorders, including various types of pain, sleep disturbances, increased anxiety, emotional instability, and behavioral disorders. Higher rates of anxiety and insomnia are observed in children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, autism spectrum disorders, and other psychiatric conditions. Early intervention that combines psychological correction with safe pharmacotherapy is critical. Given the limitations of psychopharmacological treatments in pediatric patients, standardized phytotherapy is commonly employed, particularly low-dose, multicomponent medications such as Nervoheel and Neurexan. A review of current studies suggests that Neurexan and Nervoheel are effective in managing neurotic anxiety, fears, and sleep disorders in children, and may also improve ANS dysfunction associated with emotional instability, irritability, fatigue, and senestalgia.

papers.title: Randomized Controlled Trial of Lifestyle Plus Sleep Extension Intervention on Adults With Prediabetes and Short Sleep.
papers.abstract: Short sleep duration is a modifiable barrier to diabetes prevention, yet no adequately powered trials have tested whether integrating a behavioral sleep intervention into a lifestyle intervention improves glycemic or weight loss outcomes in adults with prediabetes. To compare the effects of a lifestyle versus a lifestyle plus sleep intervention on glucose control and weight loss in adults with prediabetes and habitual short sleep duration. In this two-arm, parallel-group randomized controlled trial, adults with A1c-confirmed prediabetes and actigraphy-confirmed short sleep duration completed two clinic visits and 2-week at-home monitoring periods, including actigraphy-estimated sleep and continuous glucose monitoring. The 8-week intervention was delivered one-on-one via a Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act-compliant videoconferencing platform. The primary outcome was change in the percentage of time sensor glucose was above tight range (> 140 mg/dL). Secondary outcomes included actigraphy-estimated sleep parameters, self-reported sleep quality and daytime sleepiness, and body weight. We compared pre- to post-intervention changes between groups using a modified intention-to-treat approach. Among 196 participants, we found no significant between-group difference in the primary glucose outcome. Both groups achieved significant within-group increases in sleep and reductions in body weight, with no significant between-group differences for either outcome. The lifestyle plus sleep group showed significantly greater improvements in self-reported sleep quality and daytime sleepiness compared to the lifestyle group. Sleep onset advanced significantly only in lifestyle plus sleep group, though the between-group difference did not reach statistical significance. A post hoc analysis found that earlier sleep onset, regardless of group assignment, was independently associated with greater weight loss, whereas changes in sleep duration were not. Adding a behavioral sleep intervention to a lifestyle intervention did not improve glucose control. However, advancing sleep onset time predicted greater weight loss, independent of sleep duration or group assignment, identifying circadian timing as a promising and modifiable target for diabetes prevention. Prospective trials powered to test sleep timing interventions on metabolic outcomes are warranted.

papers.title: Framework for combined functional and computational assessment of variant pathogenicity in the sodium leak channel NALCN.
papers.abstract: The sodium leak channel nonselective (NALCN) is the pore-forming channel component of the NALCN channelosome. This protein complex generates a depolarizing sodium leak in various tissues and contributes to respiratory and circadian rhythms, locomotion, and sleep. De novo and inherited variants of NALCN can lead to severe developmental syndromes referred to as CLIFAHDD and IHPRF1, respectively. Although variants of uncertain significance (VUS) have been studied in heterologous expression systems before, there is no generally accepted framework for how to assess or predict variant pathogenicity. We functionally and computationally characterize 19 VUS detected in CLIFAHDD and IHPRF1 patients to establish a robust analysis to classify suspected disease-causing variants. Specifically, we employ multiple parameters derived from two-electrode voltage-clamp electrophysiology recordings and predicted protein stability and conservation scores. We show that this approach is capable of distinguishing benign common variants from both gain- and loss-of-function (GoF/LoF) variants. Additionally, our work provides insight into the molecular mechanism underlying specific variants and the unusual propensity of NALCN missense variants to result in GoF phenotypes. We anticipate that this experimental and computational framework will aid assessment of variant pathogenicity of NALCN and other components of the channelosome in the future.

papers.title: Infra-slow brain-heart-gut electrophysiological interactions reveal a co-ordinated multisystem physiological network in humans.
papers.abstract: Growing evidence indicates that brain continuously interacts with other physiological systems through neural and non-neural pathways. The brain-heart and brain-gut axes play a central role in homoeostasis, allostasis and behaviour, but also in cognitive aspects, including emotion and decision-making. Disruptions in these axes have been linked to a wide range of cardiovascular, neurological and psychiatric disorders. Despite this evidence, triadic crosstalk between the brain, heart and gut remains largely unexplored. Brain activity, cardiac autonomic fluctuations and gastric rhythms all exhibit slow temporal components in resting state, suggesting that brain-heart-gut electrophysiological interactions may occur over time scales from the infra-slow (0.01-0.1 Hz) physiological range. Using open-access electrophysiological recordings from 28 healthy subjects at rest, we extracted time-varying power dynamics describing the activity of the three organs: brain alpha power, cardiac sympathetic and parasympathetic indices, and the power of the gastric rhythm. Statistical associations among these organs were quantified using the maximal information coefficient across the extended temporal delay range. Physiological interactions were confirmed using surrogate-based testing, which allowed us to construct the network topology of interactions between the three organs. Our findings show that triadic brain-heart-gut interactions form a multidirectional network primarily at infra-slow time scales during resting state. This study offers one of the first insights into the physiology of brain-heart-gut interplay, providing a methodological baseline for the development of more comprehensive biomarkers based on network dynamics capable of linking pathological conditions to dysregulation across multiple organ systems. KEY POINTS: First in-human, non-invasive investigation of parallel brain-heart-gut electrophysiological interactions in awake, healthy subjects. We analysed simultaneous electroencephalographic (EEG), electrocardiographic (ECG) and electrogastrographic (EGG) recordings and quantified strength and temporal scale of the derived time series associations to construct a large-scale network of interactions. We found that brain-heart-gut interactions extend into the infra-slow range (0.01-0.1 Hz), indicating that spontaneous fluctuations in the electrophysiological activity of one organ at rest are typically followed by corresponding changes in the other two. We consistently found a robust brain-heart-gut network topology across subjects, with multidirectional interactions and bodily dynamics converging towards midline central-posterior EEG regions. These findings provide one of the first endeavours in characterizing the physiology of brain-heart-gut interactions and a methodology with strong biomarker development potential.

papers.title: Epileptic hub in MRI-negative focal cortical dysplasia using advanced dynamic statistical parametric mapping and magnetoencephalography.
papers.abstract: Localization of epileptogenic MRI-negative focal cortical dysplasia at the bottom of the sulcus (FCDB) is challenging. This study evaluated the utility of advanced dynamic statistical parametric mapping (AdSPM), a magnetoencephalography (MEG)-based source analysis method, for detecting epileptic MRI-negative FCDB. We retrospectively analyzed MEG data using AdSPM in four patients with pathologically confirmed MRI-negative FCDB, whose seizure onset zones were identified by intracranial video-EEG (IVEEG). The most active area identified by the AdSPM was designated as the AdSPM spike source. We compared the spatial concordance of the AdSPM spike source, single moving dipole (SMD) findings, and 18F-FDG PET/MRI findings with seizure onset and resection areas. An additional MRI-negative patient without seizures during IVEEG monitoring was analyzed separately for concordance with the resection area. The AdSPM spike source localized to the seizure onset zone and was included in the resection area in all four patients with an identified seizure onset zone. SMD findings were mislocalized relative to the seizure onset zone and resection area. PET/MRI was concordant with the seizure onset zone in one of three evaluable patients and with the resection area in three of four patients. In the patient without seizures during IVEEG, AdSPM and PET/MRI were concordant with the resection area; however, the SMD findings were mislocalized. AdSPM noninvasively and neurophysiologically localizes epileptic MRI-negative FCDB and may provide useful information for presurgical evaluations. This is the first diagnostic application of AdSPM for MRI-negative FCDB.

papers.title: Metabolic Barriers to Cancer Immunotherapy: Multiscale Mechanisms from Organelle Dysfunction to Organ-Specific Constraints.
papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) has reshaped cancer therapy, yet primary resistance and acquired relapse remain common despite therapeutic targeting of inhibitory receptor pathways. This limitation suggests that checkpoint release may remain insufficient when antitumor lymphocytes lack the metabolic, organelle-level, spatial, or systemic conditions required for tissue entry, functional recovery, and durable effector activity. In this review, we organize metabolic barriers to ICB into a multiscale framework comprising four interconnected axes. The Local Resource Axis captures how nutrient competition, enzymatic depletion, lipid dysregulation, suppressive metabolites, and ionic stress reshape the tumor microenvironment. The Organelle Axis examines mitochondrial dysfunction, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and intercellular mitochondrial transfer as determinants of T-cell functional recovery. The Spatial Axis addresses stromal, vascular, and organ-specific immune-metabolic niches that regulate immune access and site-specific resistance. The Systemic Axis integrates host metabolic and temporal states, including obesity, cachexia, microbial ecology, and circadian organization. Across these axes, metabolic constraints impair T-cell receptor (TCR) signaling, biosynthesis, redox homeostasis, organelle fitness, tissue infiltration, and host immune reserve, while also reducing malignant-cell susceptibility to immune-mediated killing. We further discuss therapeutic implications through a clinical-readiness and chrono-metabolic scheduling framework that distinguishes practice-ready vascular-targeted combinations from trial-prioritized or investigational dietary, microbiome-directed, metabolite-targeted, and engineered T-cell strategies. This evidence-calibrated perspective reframes tumor immunometabolism not as a static catalogue of targets, but as a set of biologically timed and compartment-specific constraints that determine the conditions under which ICB can achieve durable immune control.

papers.title: Peripartum Esketamine: A Narrative Review of Analgesia, Postpartum Depressive Symptoms, Sleep-Related Outcomes, and Safety.
papers.abstract: Pain, depressive symptoms, and sleep disruption frequently overlap during the peripartum period, although their relationships are associative rather than established as causal. Esketamine, an N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonist, has attracted interest as a peripartum intervention with potential effects on pain, mood, and sleep. This narrative review evaluates the clinical and mechanistic evidence for peripartum esketamine in analgesia, postpartum depressive symptoms, sleep-related outcomes, and maternal-infant safety, with particular attention to the directness and interpretability of the evidence. Most direct clinical evidence derives from cesarean-delivery studies, many of which are single-center trials. Evidence is most consistent for short-term analgesic benefit, whereas opioid-sparing effects are less consistent across individual studies and evidence syntheses. Several randomized trials suggest that low-dose peri-delivery esketamine may reduce early EPDS-defined screen-positive postpartum depressive symptoms, while evidence based on structured diagnostic outcomes remains limited. Evidence for sleep-related benefit remains preliminary and relies predominantly on subjective measures, with no direct postpartum polysomnographic evidence. Studied low-dose regimens have generally shown acceptable short-term maternal and neonatal tolerability in selected populations, but pregnancy-specific pharmacokinetics, lactation, and long-term offspring neurodevelopment remain insufficiently characterized. Overall, esketamine may represent an individualized adjunct in peripartum care, but current evidence does not support its routine prophylactic use. Future multicenter studies should incorporate diagnostic mood outcomes, objective sleep assessment, standardized treatment protocols, and long-term maternal and infant follow-up.

papers.title: Maternal adverse childhood experiences and epigenetic aging in pediatric populations: a scoping review.
papers.abstract: Maternal exposure to adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) may influence aging biomarkers in pediatric populations, as estimated using epigenetic clocks or other measures of aging, such as telomere length. This scoping review aimed to identify and map the available evidence on the association between maternal ACEs and biomarkers of epigenetic aging in offspring from birth to 18 years of age. A systematic search of MEDLINE, Embase, APA PsycINFO, CINAHL, Scopus, and ProQuest Dissertations and Theses Global was conducted on 26 May 2025 and updated on 28 April 2026. The inclusion criteria were epigenetic clock studies that included pediatric populations (0-18 years of age) born to mothers who self-reported ACEs during gestation or within 1 year after childbirth using a standard questionnaire. DNA methylation analysis was conducted using biospecimens, and offspring aging biomarkers were examined. Three reviewers independently screened 1,441 articles, of which 38 underwent full-text review. Four studies met our inclusion criteria. The geographic scope of the studies was limited; three studies were conducted in the United States and one in the United Kingdom. Sample sizes ranged from 80 to 883 maternal-child dyads. The age at the time of biological sample collection ranged from birth to 8 years. Measures of epigenetic aging were examined across diverse tissue types, including blood, saliva, and umbilical vein endothelial cells. Some evidence has been found for an association between maternal ACEs and offspring epigenetic aging; however, the findings were often limited to specific conditions or ACE subtypes. Total maternal ACE scores were not significantly associated with newborn gestational epigenetic age acceleration or child symptoms. However, more specific associations emerged for maternal experiences of parental divorce, sexual abuse, and neglect. In addition, sex-specific associations were also noted. Racial disparities were also evident with maternal childhood abuse linked to increased epigenetic aging in Black but not White maternal-child dyads. Some associations emerged only when considering moderators such as maternal restless sleep during pregnancy. Maternal ACEs may influence offspring epigenetic aging; however, these associations are complex, context-dependent, and supported by a limited body of evidence. Longitudinal studies with greater demographic diversity and methodological consistency, alongside mechanistic investigations of the biological pathways linking maternal adversity and offspring epigenetic aging, are needed.
papers.journal: Frontiers in child and adolescent psychiatry

papers.title: Rapid Improvement of Persistent Catatonia Temporally Associated With Amantadine After Benzodiazepine Intolerance and Discontinuation of Electroconvulsive Therapy: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Catatonia can be difficult to manage when benzodiazepines are poorly tolerated, and electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) cannot be continued. We report the case of a 23-year-old woman with a schizophrenia-spectrum disorder and catatonia presenting with mutism, delayed responses, staring, posturing, waxy flexibility, withdrawal, and abnormal behavior. Treatment with lorazepam was limited by excessive sedation. She then received four bitemporal ECT sessions before she and her mother declined further ECT due to reported adverse effects. Soon after discharge, she was found wandering outside while confused and required readmission. Nine days after her last ECT session, her Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (BFCRS) severity score was 11. Amantadine 100 mg twice daily was started, and three days later her BFCRS severity score fell to 3, a 72.7% reduction. Because her altered mental status persisted, a neurologic evaluation was performed. Brain MRI, routine electroencephalography (EEG), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies, infectious testing, and neuronal autoantibody testing, including N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antibody testing, were unremarkable. Amantadine was then increased to 200 mg twice daily, and zolpidem 5 mg nightly was later added. Her final BFCRS severity score was 2. Although delayed ECT effects, concurrent treatment of the underlying psychotic disorder, spontaneous fluctuation, and subsequent interventions preclude causal attribution, this case shows rapid, objectively measured improvement temporally associated with the start of amantadine treatment.

papers.title: Follicular development impairment in polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome: multidimensional pathophysiological networks and frontier therapeutic targets.
papers.abstract: Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) is a prevalent endocrine-metabolic disorder characterised by follicular arrest, anovulation, and elevated androgen levels. This review transcends single-dimensional analyses of PMOS pathology from neuroendocrine or metabolic perspectives, proposing an integrated multi-layered network model to systematically elucidate the pathological mechanisms underlying follicular arrest. Post-pubertal dysfunction of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis interacts with systemic metabolic dysregulation, jointly establishing an ovarian microenvironment characterised by hyperandrogenism, hyperinsulinaemia, and chronic inflammation. This environment further induces self-reinforcing vicious cycles within follicles, manifesting as impaired granulosa-oocyte communication, immunometabolic reprogramming (e.g., M1 macrophage polarisation), and organelle stress (including mitochondrial dysfunction and endoplasmic reticulum stress). This localised cycle is consolidated and amplified by higher-level regulatory factors-including developmental epigenetic programming, the gut-brain-ovary axis, and circadian rhythms-ultimately establishing a pathologically entrenched state. Finally, this network-based understanding informs future research pathways, focusing on how emerging strategies-such as multi-omics integration, artificial intelligence, and stem cell secretome studies-can advance phenotype-directed precision interventions. This review aims to provide a systematic, dynamic theoretical framework for understanding the complex pathogenesis of PMOS and its potential therapeutic targets.

papers.title: Performance in play: stimulant exposure and broader substance-use vulnerability in mass-participation youth esports.
papers.abstract: Youth esports now extends far beyond professional competition, encompassing ranked online play, school clubs, amateur events, livestreaming, and digitally mediated peer communities. These settings expose adolescents to energy drinks and other stimulant-containing products in contexts where alertness, concentration, and prolonged play are valued. Energy drinks merit particular attention because their prominence in gaming culture combines caffeine exposure with, for many products, substantial added sugar. Potential consequences include disrupted sleep, acute stimulant effects, and adverse nutritional and metabolic profiles. A further concern is behavioral: repeated consumption for gaming-related fatigue or concentration may foster expectations that psychoactive products are useful tools for performance. Research on nonmedical prescription-stimulant use among adolescents demonstrates a comparable performance-oriented motive, while longitudinal studies link energy-drink use with later tobacco, alcohol, and other substance involvement. These associations remain non-causal and have not been established specifically in recreational esports. This Perspective frames mass-participation youth esports as an emerging setting for early public-health intervention. It proposes action across marketing and sponsorship, schools and community programs, beverage and product policy, families and healthcare, and longitudinal surveillance, while emphasizing the need to establish prevalence, temporal ordering, and high-risk patterns directly in nonprofessional adolescent participants across different social and regulatory settings.

papers.title: KAT6A-Mutant iPSC-Derived Cortical Neurons Display Precocious Maturation, Dysregulated Electrophysiology, and Altered Morphology.
papers.abstract: KAT6A syndrome is a complex neurodevelopmental disorder caused by heterozygous pathogenic KAT6A variants inflicting variable degrees of developmental delay and intellectual disability via a mechanism that remains largely uncharacterized. To further our understanding, we differentiated KAT6A syndrome patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells into neural progenitor cells and cortical neurons. KAT6A syndrome patient-derived cells exhibit an altered transcriptome, with many of the dysregulated genes associated with autism spectrum disorder. At an early stage of differentiation, KAT6A-mutant cortical neurons show many elevated neurodevelopment-specific genes, including key transcription factors. Detailed electrophysiological measurements uncover that KAT6A-mutant cortical neurons display a hyperexcitability phenotype at an early stage of differentiation, followed by hypoexcitability at a later stage, compared with control neurons. These electrophysiological alterations were accompanied by decreased sodium and potassium currents. Remarkably, early KAT6A-mutant neurons exhibit a markedly lower percentage of GABA-positive neurons and increased spontaneous calcium activity as compared with control neurons. Moreover, multiple morphometric alterations in early-stage KAT6A-mutant cortical neurons indicate premature maturation, including increased neurite outgrowth, arbor complexity and soma size. Consistently, KAT6A knockout SH-SY5Y cells exhibit impaired differentiation capability and dysregulated gene expression. These novel findings establish the deleterious impact of pathogenic KAT6A variants on cortical neuron differentiation and electrophysiological function.

papers.title: The developmental dopamine trajectory hypothesis of ADHD across the lifespan.
papers.abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is increasingly recognized as a lifespan neurodevelopmental disorder, yet the mechanisms underlying its changing clinical presentation across development remain poorly understood. Although childhood ADHD is typically characterized by hyperactivity, impulsivity, and inattention, symptom expression frequently evolves during adolescence and adulthood toward greater reward dysregulation, executive dysfunction, motivational impairment, internal restlessness, and changing manifestations of emotional dysregulation. Existing neurobiological models have substantially advanced understanding of ADHD pathophysiology but provide limited explanation for how symptom continuity can coexist with developmental changes in clinical expression. Here, we propose the Developmental Dopamine Trajectory Hypothesis, which posits that DAT related dopaminergic dysregulation may interact with the sequential maturation of frontostriatal, mesolimbic, and mesocortical circuits to contribute to developmental changes in ADHD symptom expression across the lifespan. A central proposition of the framework is that the functional consequences of DAT related dopaminergic dysregulation depend on the developmental state of the neural circuits on which it acts. Within this framework, childhood manifestations may arise primarily from interactions between dopaminergic vulnerability and developing frontostriatal networks, adolescent manifestations from increasing involvement of reward and emotion related circuitry, and adult manifestations from interactions with mature executive control and motivational systems. By integrating evidence from longitudinal clinical studies, neuroimaging, electrophysiology, pharmacology, genetics, and translational DAT models, the proposed framework provides a mechanistic model for how developmental changes in neural circuit state may contribute to changing symptom expression despite continuity of underlying neurobiological vulnerability. The hypothesis generates testable predictions regarding longitudinal symptom trajectories, developmental biomarker changes, potential developmental differences in treatment responsiveness, and adolescence as a proposed critical neurodevelopmental transition period. Reconceptualizing ADHD through a developmental dopaminergic framework places developmental timing and neural circuit maturation at the center of the relationship between dopaminergic vulnerability and clinical phenotype, providing a basis for future longitudinal, mechanistic, and developmentally informed research across the lifespan.

papers.title: Persistent Sleepiness After Effective Positive Airway Pressure Therapy Deserves Independent Clinical Evaluation.
papers.abstract: Positive airway pressure (PAP) therapy often improves excessive daytime sleepiness in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), yet effective control of sleep-disordered breathing does not invariably restore normal daytime alertness. Persistent sleepiness after PAP therapy should therefore be regarded as a clinical observation requiring explanation rather than automatically attributed to treated OSA. The term "residual excessive daytime sleepiness" may become misleading when it is interpreted as an etiologic conclusion rather than a descriptive label. Evaluation should distinguish PAP adherence from treatment efficacy and symptomatic recovery, determine whether the complaint reflects sleepiness rather than fatigue or apathy, and consider alternative contributors including insufficient sleep, circadian misalignment, medication or substance effects, medical and psychiatric conditions, coexisting sleep disorders, and central disorders of hypersomnolence. Additional testing should be guided by a defined clinical question, and wake-promoting therapy should follow rather than replace diagnostic reassessment. Persistent sleepiness after effective PAP describes an observation, not an etiology, and deserves independent clinical evaluation.

papers.title: Alzheimer's disease risk gene Wwox controls amyloid pathology through metabolic reprogramming.
papers.abstract: Genome-wide association studies have identified multiple loci that contribute to late-onset Alzheimer's disease risk, yet the functional mechanisms of many candidate genes remain unclear. WW-domain containing oxidoreductase (WWOX) is one such gene associated with disease and downregulated in patient brains, but its role in neurodegeneration is poorly understood. Here, we use Drosophila models to investigate the cell-type-specific and mechanistic roles of Wwox in ageing and amyloid-β42 (Aβ42)-induced pathology. Neuronal and glial knockdown of Wwox reduced lifespan and increased sleep drive, indicating a role in brain homeostasis. In an Aβ42 transgenic model, neuronal Wwox knockdown exacerbated toxicity, shortening lifespan, impairing locomotion, and increasing soluble Aβ42 levels. Transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses revealed that Wwox knockdown in an Aβ42 transgenic model promotes metabolic reprogramming, characterized by elevated lactate dehydrogenase (Ldh) expression and increased lactate levels, driven by activation of the stress-responsive transcription factor Atf4. Genetic reduction of Ldh rescued locomotor deficits, identifying dysregulated pyruvate metabolism as a key mediator of Wwox-dependent neurotoxicity. Conversely, overexpression of Wwox in neurons markedly reduced amyloid burden, improved survival and locomotor function, and reversed Aβ42-induced transcriptional changes. Both Aβ42 and the protective effects of Wwox were associated with altered amino acid metabolism, including changes in the cysteine and L-methionine pathway. Together, these findings identify WWOX as a regulator of neuronal metabolic state, linking genetic risk to amyloid pathology via metabolic reprogramming, and highlight WWOX activation as a potential therapeutic strategy in Alzheimer's disease.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in cardiology: an evidence map across subspecialties, 2014-26.
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied in healthcare, including cardiology, with growing interest in its potential to support diagnosis, prognosis, and clinical decision-making. The rapid pace of technological advancements is not matched by equivalent progress in the regulation and appraisal of these systems. This review aims to provide a structured evidence map of AI models in cardiology, by grading the robustness of clinical validation and mapping it against the quantity of publications across main subspecialties. To assess the strength of evidence, we defined, developed, and applied a novel classification tailored for AI models that ranks evidence into five Grades of Validation according to the level of clinical validity. We screened literature from 2014 to 2026 according to the PRISMA guidelines, identifying a total of 2807 articles on AI applications within cardiology, 490 of which met the inclusion criteria (validation was performed in at least one external, independent patient population), revealing a highly heterogeneous distribution of evidence across subspecialties. Most studies in AI focused on improved diagnostics (n = 322, 65.7%); however, advanced integration in prognostic (n = 122, 24.9%) and therapeutic applications remains limited (n = 46, 9.4%). Cardiovascular imaging leads AI applications, especially in coronary computed tomography and echocardiography, followed by non-invasive electrophysiology, predominantly in atrial fibrillation screening and ventricular dysfunction detection. The scarcity of prospective validations across different resources and geographical settings (n = 134, 27.3%) and randomized controlled trials (n = 35, 3.8%) limits the adoption by clinical guidelines and widespread implementation of AI algorithms.

papers.title: Hemodynamics, plasma catecholamines, and power spectral analysis of heart rate variability during tilt-evoked neurally mediated hypotension.
papers.abstract: Syncope workup often includes tilt table testing. One positive result is neurally mediated hypotension (NMH). Mechanisms of NMH are debated. We characterized NMH development in terms of systemic and forearm hemodynamics, plasma catecholamines, and power spectral analysis of heart rate variability. We reviewed data from 25 subjects with NMH and 34 controls without NMH who had autonomic testing between 2003 and 2024. Dependent measures included continuously recorded blood pressure (BP), heart rate, stroke volume, cardiac output, respiratory rate (RR), forearm blood flow (FBF), forearm vascular resistance (FVR), systemic vascular resistance (SVR), plasma epinephrine and norepinephrine, and high- and low-frequency power of heart rate variability (HFRR and LFRR). There were 4 study periods: T0 = supine rest; T1 = start of tilt; T2 = NMH (20 min of tilting in controls); and T3 = supine recovery. There were significant interaction effects for Group X Study Period for several variables, with a decrease in BP, FVR, SVR, HFRR, and LFRR, and an increase in FBF and epinephrine at a steeper rate in the NMH group compared to the No NMH group. The two groups did not differ in responses of heart rate, RR, stroke volume, cardiac output, or norepinephrine levels. The increment in plasma epinephrine was larger in the NMH group, without a group difference in norepinephrine (i.e., sympathoadrenal imbalance). LFRR was elevated at baseline and decreased markedly in participants developing NMH. NMH is associated with forearm vasodilation, sympathoadrenal imbalance, and a precipitous fall in LFRR. The results fit with a neurocirculatory-neuroendocrine pattern triggering NMH.

papers.title: Circadian rhythms in health and disease.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms, serving as a crucial temporal bridge linking neural activity and pathological biology, are regulated by central pacemaker neurons to maintain cellular homeostasis and coordinate diverse biological processes. Circadian rhythm disruption is closely associated with various diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders, metabolic disorders, and cancer. Circadian rhythms are controlled by core clock genes, such as BMAL1 and CLOCK, modulating numerous physiological processes, encompassing metabolism, immune responses, neural activity, and hormone regulation. Circadian rhythms disruptions arising from shift work, jet lag, or inconsistent sleep schedules are implicated in both the onset and progression of numerous diseases, notably Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. The article highlights how circadian dysregulation alters cellular processes to potentially accelerate disease progression. Circadian disruption results in impaired immune function, further promoting disease development and resistance to treatment. Potential therapeutic applications based on circadian biology, such as chronotherapy and personalized medicine, are also discussed. Recent technological advances, embodied in wearable devices and omics approaches, are increasingly providing deeper insights into circadian biology. Further unveiling the role of circadian in health and disease opens new avenues for tailoring treatment timing to patients' biological rhythms, thereby enhancing therapeutic outcomes across various diseases. By bridging fundamental circadian mechanisms with clinical pathology, this review provides a roadmap for future chronotherapeutic interventions in precision medicine.

papers.title: Polysocial risk score predicts chronic kidney disease incidence and prognosis: mechanistic insights from plasma metabolome, proteome and lifestyle.
papers.abstract: The cumulative impact of multiple social determinants of health (SDHs) on chronic kidney disease (CKD) remains poorly understood. This prospective study examined the association of a polysocial risk score (PsRS) with CKD incidence and subsequent risks of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and mortality, and explored potential mediating pathways via multi-omics profiling and lifestyle factors. We analyzed 279,548 participants free of CKD at baseline and 19,761 patients with established CKD in the UK Biobank. The PsRS integrated 15 factors across economic, educational, healthcare, neighborhood, and social domains. Plasma metabolomic and proteomic profiles were analyzed to identify omics signatures associated with the PsRS. An unhealthy lifestyle score (uHLS) was derived based on body mass index, smoking, alcohol consumption, physical activity, sleep, and diet. Cox proportional hazards models were used to assess associations between the PsRS and outcomes. Mediation analyses were performed in subsets with available omics and lifestyle data. Over a median follow-up of 13 years, 6,628 incident CKD cases, 3,724 CVD events, and 2,486 deaths were documented. The PsRS demonstrated a positive association with incident CKD risk among CKD-free participants (per 1-point increase: HR=1.12; 95% CI: 1.11-1.14), as well as with CVD (HR=1.08; 95% CI: 1.07-1.10) and all-cause mortality (HR=1.12; 95% CI: 1.10-1.14) in CKD patients. The PsRS significantly improved the predictive performance of conventional clinical models across all outcomes, as indicated by increases in the C-index, net reclassification improvement, and integrated discrimination improvement. Multi-omics analyses revealed a PsRS-associated metabolomic signature (94 metabolites primarily involved in amino acids, fatty acids, and lipoproteins) and a proteomic signature (428 proteins primarily involved in immune/inflammatory responses, cellular signaling, and fibrosis).
